items.title: Apple’s iPhone camera leader has reportedly left the company
items.summary: Jon McCormack, Apple's vice president of camera software engineering, left the company last month, Bloomberg reports. Its sources say McCormack retired "at the end of October after more than eight years at the company." Apple reportedly has not yet named a new VP to step in for M
items.content:
Bloomberg reports Jon McCormack retired last month, continuing Apple’s recent leadership shuffle.

Jon McCormack, Apple’s vice president of camera software engineering, left the company last month, Bloomberg reports . Its sources say McCormack retired “at the end of October after more than eight years at the company.” Apple reportedly has not yet named a new VP to step in for McCormack, who oversaw its Camera and Photos apps, and the tech that defined generations of photos and the photography and editing experience on Apple’s devices.

McCormack played a major role in defining how iPhone photos look, and he was always ready to get into the weeds with reporters after iPhone events. In 2024, he told The Verge that Apple sees a photo as “a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened.”

The departure follows John Ternus taking over for Tim Cook as Apple’s CEO in September. Apple has had other major leadership changes recently, including Phil Schiller stepping down as head of the App Store and Apple events and Steve Smith stepping in as the company’s new M&A and corporate development boss.

items.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
items.summary: Google's latest update to Gemini brings an AI agent to the Mac that can organize files, fill out forms, and tackle multistep workflows.
items.content:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps and browsing websites in the background.

The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.

Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September , which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.

Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent being able to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multi-step tasks that involve getting things done across the local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.

As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.

Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.

The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

items.title: Google will launch Android app verification requirement globally in January 2027
items.summary: Google says almost all developers have already gotten on board with verification.
items.content:
Google announced Android developer verification last year , and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead . It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven’t registered their apps to do so soon.

The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won’t be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure . Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.

In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it’s not wasting any time with the January start. It says that verification will reach all devices within “several months.”

So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with “millions” of non-Play apps already registered. The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

The verifier system service has already been rolled out to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or higher, which accounts for just about every Android device in the world outside of China and Russia. Google has also partnered with the biggest third-party app stores to enforce verification: Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion, and Vivo. The system-level verifier is responsible for blocking installs, but these stores will only list verified apps once Google flips the switch.

Google has gotten a lot of feedback since announcing this change, and it has listened to some of it. Hobbyists will be able to register a free account to distribute apps to a small group. Google initially planned to limit this to 25 total installs, but that has since been increased to 50 installs. There’s also now an API that developers can use to streamline registering new application packages.

Google also relented and created an opt-out system for users who don’t want their installations limited. The so-called “ advanced flow ” will let you install whatever you want regardless of verification status, but it’s not a simple toggle. The option will be buried, and there will be plenty of scary warnings about the risks. You’ll also have to wait 24 hours to fully activate the feature.

Even if Google has managed to make verification a little more warm and cuddly, it still gives the company a lot more control. Developers in sanctioned nations won’t be able to verify their identities , locking them out of app distribution. Sideloading an app may also require a Google server connection. Only popular app IDs will be cached on devices for verification purposes. For others, your phone will have to check with Google before installing. These will be edge cases, certainly, but still very annoying ones.

As Google moves toward full verification enforcement, it has created guides for developers and app distributors to outline all the salient points. These guides suggest Google expects verification to be fully online by March 1, 2027.

items.title: Amazon is pushing alerts opposing NYC’s Delivery Protection Act
items.summary: Amazon is serving up push notifications and banners on its home page to some users, warning that a new bill could add up to $5 per order in New York City. The Delivery Protection Act, which is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani and a number of labor groups, including the Teamsters, w
items.content:
Amazon claims that a new bill could add $5 per order for New Yorkers.

Amazon is serving up push notifications and banners on its home page to some users, warning that a new bill could add up to $5 per order in New York City. The Delivery Protection Act, which is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani and a number of labor groups, including the Teamsters, would require Amazon to employ its current fleet of third-party delivery contractors directly.

Currently, Amazon turns to a network of small delivery companies that often work exclusively with the retailer. This is why your packages are dropped off by a guy in a Toyota Camry sometimes, rather than an Amazon truck. The new bill would require that last-mile delivery firms be licensed by the city and directly employed, rather than operate as contractors.

Next to Black Friday deal offers, now Amazon is showing a big tile with a red banner that says, “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Other users are reporting similar notices in the mobile app and after completing orders .

In a statement posted to its site, Amazon says that:

If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them [third-party delivery contractors], and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

Mayor Mandani and labor unions have countered that the current subcontractor model allows corporations like Amazon to avoid accountability and exploit vulnerable workers .

Amazon’s threats to leave New York to avoid regulation and efforts to unionize within the city follows shortly after the company’s third-quarter earnings report in which it said that it was on its way to having not one, but two trillion-dollar businesses in the next five to ten years.

items.title: The only software that didn’t break this week...
Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and exposing private data, report says
items.summary: In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn't belong to them.
items.content:
Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

In another example, an employee using the AI agent on her personal phone received a reminder from Muse to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, the popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post, according to the report.

Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

Meta did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

items.content:
At $129.99, it’s just $10 more than the base Kindle, only with a bunch of extra features.

alt: Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite is just $10 more than the base model alt: The last-gen Kindle Paperwhite for $130 is a stellar Black Friday deal

Amazon debuted its latest Kindle Paperwhite in October, which is now available for $199.99 and replaces the outgoing 2024 model. However, given the minimal improvements on the new model — it’s a little thinner and opens books faster — the last-gen Paperwhite is still one of the best e-readers you can buy. And now, the latter is down to $129.99 ($70 off), nearly its lowest price ever, at Amazon , Best Buy , and Target .

Some important pricing context: The waterproof e-reader held steady at $159.99 until late August, when its price rose 25 percent due to rising component costs ( many other Amazon tech products got more expensive, too). Even if the price hike never happened, though, this would still be a nice discount.

The $129.99 Paperwhite includes 16GB of storage and features lockscreen ads (it costs $20 extra to opt out at checkout), just like the newer version. It also packs a sharp 300ppi display with adjustable color temperature and USB-C charging. If you want more features — including twice the storage, zero ads, wireless charging, and an auto-adjusting front light — opt instead for the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition while it’s down to $179.99 (also $70 off), which is just $10 shy of its best price to date.

For the sake of being comprehensive, the last-gen base Kindle is going for $119.99 ($30 off) at Amazon ahead of Black Friday. While the standard Kindle has improved with each new iteration, it’s tough to recommend when the vastly superior Paperwhite is on sale for just $10 more. That 10 bucks gets you so much: waterproofing, better battery life, faster page-turning speeds, and a higher pixel density screen that’s slightly larger (7 inches vs. 6 inches).

items.title: Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents
items.summary: The company’s alternate-universe internet serves as a massive sandbox that allows the Chrome team to properly train AI browsing agents—without the risk of them going rogue.
items.content:
As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models , they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea . That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks , to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see, the exploration space that we have to address is huge and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgement when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity checks so the agents could have a normal experience. The team emphasizes, though, that none of these attacks would be possible against regular Chrome users on the open internet. They were all facilitated by the god-mode type access and privilege the team inherently has because they control the entire environment and network.

The researchers say that while the browsing assistant agents they have been testing are benign and do not have cyber capabilities, their goal is to make the Mirror Dimension available to teams across Google so more researchers have access to the safe and controlled environment for testing.

“We’re sharing this approach so other teams both internally and externally think about doing it this way,” says Doug Turner, Google’s director of engineering. “This is the first step, there’s going to be continued investment in this approach to train models. And I would imagine as they become more sophisticated we’ll have to continue working on this environment to make it more and more realistic.”

items.title: Anthropic hits Nasdaq exchanges at $111, 33% above IPO price
items.summary: Anthropic's IPO price was set at $83, representing more than $80 billion in new capital raised.
items.content:
Shares of Anthropic are now trading on the Nasdaq exchange, as the company successfully executes its initial public offering. In the early minutes of availability, shares were trading at $111.50, a 33% premium over the $83 IPO price.

Set on Wednesday, the IPO price was already higher than the projected range set by the company, which anticipated a price between $70 and $78 per share. All told, the offering will raise over $81 billion, directed to a combination of employees and the company’s own coffers.

The IPO funding, together with existing fundraising and new private offerings timed to coincide with the company’s public market debut, will leave Anthropic with an expected $220 billion in cash reserves. As one analyst told TechCrunch , “Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had.”

The share price continues to fluctuate, but the opening price would put the company’s market cap over $2 trillion, making it more valuable than Meta, Tesla, or Walmart. Only five companies boast a higher valuation by market cap: Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft.

In a speech before the opening bell , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized the company’s commitment to safety. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.”

items.title: Anthropic starts trading on Wall Street
items.summary: Anthropic has officially gone public. It began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" at $111.50 per share, up from its initial $83 per share price that put company's value at around $1.5 trillion. The listing comes nearly a month after Anthropic revealed its plans t
items.content:
Anthropic began trading at $111.50 / share.

Anthropic has officially gone public. It began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT” at $111.50 per share , up from its initial $83 per share price that put company’s value at around $1.5 trillion.

The listing comes nearly a month after Anthropic revealed its plans to go public . In its lengthy S-1 filing, the AI company reported recording an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of this year, most of which comes from an accounting charge that doesn’t reflect its business, along with $16.3 billion in revenue. The filing outlines plans that Anthropic says will help it develop AI for the benefit of humanity, which includes a governance structure that keeps control of the company in the hands of the founders, rather than the shareholders.

While speaking ahead of Anthropic’s debut at the Nasdaq, CEO Dario Amodei highlighted his stance on AI safety. “To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei said, according to Reuters . “We will not bend to either business nor political pressure.”

Anthropic’s S-1 filing also listed possible “catastrophic” risks associated with its AI models, including “self-preserving behaviors” like resisting attempts to shut them down. It also warns potential shareholders that its AI models “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that can harm Anthropic.

Anthropic recently revealed that, like rival OpenAI, it has experienced incidents of AI agents escaping their testing environment and hacking third-party organizations . In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a plan to slow down the training and development of AI in response to the wave of rogue AI cyberattacks. As part of that plan, it gave safety evaluators at METR “employee-like access” to its internal systems, who found that the company is using AI to accelerate its research and development.

items.title: Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app
items.summary: In 2015 Microsoft acquired a to-do list app called Wunderlist, for a price rumored to be as high as $200 million. Wunderlist fans were worried that Microsoft would make their beloved app soulless and corporate, or worse, hide it behind some convoluted enterprise subscription. But
items.content:
The Wunderlist era is officially over. Good luck getting your stuff out.

In 2015 Microsoft acquired a to-do list app called Wunderlist, for a price rumored to be as high as $200 million. Wunderlist fans were worried that Microsoft would make their beloved app soulless and corporate, or worse, hide it behind some convoluted enterprise subscription. But against all odds, Microsoft was a good steward: The app became Microsoft To Do , but it remained a useful and powerful way for people to manage their tasks across all platforms.

Now Microsoft is pulling the rug. Buried deep in a blog post about “unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365” is the news that the To Do apps will “retire” on June 30th, 2027. The transition will be painful: Starting next summer, business users will need to use the Planner app for their tasks, but Microsoft won’t migrate their tasks automatically. And personal users, well, don’t let the door hit you. “Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app,” the blog post reads.

From a certain strategic standpoint, you can almost see how this makes sense. (Microsoft hasn’t responded to a request for comment.) It’s definitely true that Microsoft’s task- and project-management offerings are too complicated; To Do and Planner have some overlapping features, and you can use a half-dozen different Microsoft apps to manage your daily tasks. Microsoft has been hinting at bringing everything under the Planner banner for some time, and as Microsoft tries to foist Copilot upon everything you do at work, bringing all that stuff into one place makes more sense.

(“More sense” may be relative, though. When your blog post contains sentences like, “Additionally, this unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier because it’s all part of Work IQ,” you still have some work to do.)

It’s also yet another sign that Microsoft is simply giving up on the idea of making software that people use outside of work. Planner isn’t available through a personal or family Microsoft 365 account, so you can’t switch if you want to. Not that you necessarily would: Lots of people liked To Do specifically because it was a list of tasks, not a project management platform. Planner is a business tool for business users, administered by IT professionals and monitored by big bosses.

Planner is also, in many ways, just not as good a platform. It doesn’t have a dedicated desktop app — you’re meant to use it on the web, or through Teams or Outlook — and is missing some of To Do’s useful syncing and sharing features. Microsoft is not promising to spend the next six months closing those gaps, or even offering to help people export their data and move on. The company is simply getting all the way out of the business of helping regular people manage their days, and leaving users in the lurch.

If you’re suddenly shopping for a new to-do list, the good news is there are plenty of good options. Todoist and TickTick are the two stalwarts of the space, and they offer much of the same ubiquity and simplicity as To Do (though I agree with all the commenters on Reddit and Microsoft’s blog , who say To Do’s interface was better than either one.) Google Tasks is being integrated across Google’s own office suite. The vibe coding revolution has also persuaded approximately every person on the internet to build their own to-do app, so you have lots to choose from. At this point, there’s seemingly only one company left that doesn’t want you managing your days and tasks in its systems, and it’s Microsoft.

items.title: At Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO recommits to pacing AI development
items.summary: In his Nasdaq opening bell speech, Dario Amodei reiterated Anthropic's commitment to pacing AI development, regardless of business or political pressure.
items.content:
As Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday in the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing AI responsibly. In his speech ahead of the Nasdaq opening bell, Amodei vowed that the AI company would not bend to either business or political pressure and would “remain under human control.”

Reading the speech from a printout, the CEO began by talking about Anthropic’s origins as a way to build powerful technology to help humanity — something that he said was inspired by the loss of his father to a disease that became curable just a few years later.

He acknowledged that while human intelligence had made diseases like the plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world, there were still too few scientists with too little time to make progress in other areas of disease. AI, he said, could help with this by working in concert with humans to further medical progress.

It’s telling that Amodei began with a story highlighting AI’s potentially lifesaving applications, since he’s warned repeatedly about the risks of advancing the technology too quickly. In September, Amodei drew headlines when he outlined a plan to pace AI development , which included things like coordinating with other leading companies on safety standards and embedding evaluators from third-party organizations to verify that companies were following their safety commitments.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, and xAI owner Elon Musk said they agreed with Amodei’s position, although few concrete commitments have been made.

In this morning’s speech, Amodei again stressed the need to progress AI technology and the safety required in doing so. He referred to the “very real risks” of AI in the hands of bad actors, whether those were individuals or nation-states, and the potential for things like “economic disruption” and “losing control of AI systems.”

Anthropic believes these risks are avoidable, he noted, as long as there are safeguards in place. Amodei said the company would continue to be invested in the work of AI alignment and testing, and developing new ways to understand AI behavior so it could remain under human control.

“There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us,” he said. “The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double and triple checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.”

“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei concluded.

His sister, Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, echoed these sentiments in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, noting that while the risks were real, the promise of AI was also “incredible.”

“We were really founded on this idea that it is our job to mitigate those risks, and I think we have to date done an incredible job doing that. We obviously have more work ahead of us, but we are deeply committed to safety,” she added. The full text of Dario Amodei’s opening speech is below:

Thank you, Daniela. My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind. Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that just a few years later became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments. So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket — tools for gene editing, tools for gene synthesis, tools for controlling brain cells with light — started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking, from intelligence.

Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades. It took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR. Nature is full of these patterns, but we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them. Too few scientists with too [little] time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would have taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point, all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time, and although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe these processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by a few years. Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many other applications of Claude. Our customers, the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people, are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth, lift people out of poverty, protect democracy and free societies, even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them, and I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

items.title: The best things in open source are built together
items.summary: Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion. The post The best things in open source are built together appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
items.content:
In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion , more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities.

Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine.

Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica , an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework .

I attended John Maeda and Qianqian Ye’s session at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed.

This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked:

“What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?”

“I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.”

In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica , which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit.

GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground

With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate.

With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit.

Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all.

As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub has to offer.

The Open Source Accessibility Framework, created in collaboration with external contributors from the disability and accessibility communities, launched last month. It helps make accessibility an inherent part of how projects are created. It is an accountability model with four phases so developers can turn projects and accessibility goals into public, trackable progress. A core component of this is the new ACCESSIBILITY.md file, a file now visible on repository overview pages, giving a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. Read more about the ACCESSIBILITY.md file.

Going back to John and Qianqian’s Universe talk, John asked:

“How does an open source community keep something lasting that long? What’s the secret?”

“I think the secret is one of the most obvious ones. Community.”

The GitHub repo firstcontributions/first-contributions ranked fourth among the fastest-growing community projects in 2026 by contributors, helping developers take their first steps into open source. We hope you can join our open-source community: hack away at our new projects or start your own.

Watch John Maeda and Qianqian Ye’s session 👇

In the Codename MDASH pilot, GitHub and Microsoft turned thousands of raw AI findings into 99 checked, private reports with suggested fixes for six widely used open source projects. Maintainers have already fixed more than half.

Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.

items.title: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order
items.summary: The U.K. tribunal's ruling rejected London's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
items.content:
The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information.

The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret.

The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.

The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort , arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.

California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.

Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. A spokesperson for Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment following the ruling, but previously told TechCrunch that the company has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”

A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.

Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.

A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.

items.title: ChatGPT can transcribe as you speak now with Live Dictation
items.summary: ChatGPT can receive audio prompts from your microphone faster now with a Live Dictation feature that transcribes as you speak, rather than waiting until you finish recording. It's rolling out now globally on all ChatGPT plans on the web, desktop app, and iOS and Android apps. Whi
items.content:
ChatGPT’s new Live Dictation feature transcribes audio prompts faster, with no more 10-minute limit.﻿

ChatGPT can receive audio prompts from your microphone faster now with a Live Dictation feature that transcribes as you speak, rather than waiting until you finish recording. It’s rolling out now globally on all ChatGPT plans on the web, desktop app, and iOS and Android apps. While using dictation in ChatGPT, you can tap or click the audio waveform to show the live text transcript the AI is generating, then edit it in the prompt box when you’re done.

Along with faster transcription, OpenAI also announced it’s removing the 10-minute recording limit on voice dictation in ChatGPT, and it says the feature is getting “more reliable.” The update follows an overhaul for ChatGPT’s two-way conversational voice mode earlier this year. Last year, OpenAI also announced a “record mode” for transcribing voice notes and meetings. That feature is still in beta and limited to Plus, Enterprise, Edu, Business, and Pro workspaces, but you can also use ChatGPT’s prompt box dictation feature to ask it to transcribe voice messages or turn them into bullet points.
